2.1a — Coins: Triggers, Colliders & the StatManager

Movement gets you around the world; now it is time to interact with it. Today you learn how Unity detects when two objects overlap, how to set up a coin with trigger colliders, and how to build a StatManager from scratch to keep score.

Read the Docs ~15 min

In real life, two solid objects cannot occupy the same space. In a physics engine, detecting when shapes touch requires Colliders. But not all collisions are meant to stop you like a brick wall. Pickups like coins should let you walk right through them while recording an event.

Unity provides a special mode on 2D colliders called Is Trigger:

  • Solid Collider (Is Trigger = unchecked): Bumps and blocks. Unity's physics engine stops the objects from penetrating.
  • Trigger Collider (Is Trigger = checked): Intangible zone. Objects pass freely through each other, and Unity fires the OnTriggerEnter2D message.

When two objects overlap and at least one is a trigger, Unity executes this method:

private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other)

Notice the parameter: Collider2D other. When the player runs into a coin, who is other? other is the collider belonging to the coin!

Socratic: Reading Unity Functions for Identification

When OnTriggerEnter2D fires, it fires for anything the player walks into — grass, doorways, hazards, or coins. How do we know what we just touched? Read these two ways to check in Unity:

ApproachExampleHow It Works
CompareTagother.CompareTag("Coin")Optimized engine check. Validates the tag name and produces zero garbage collection memory.
tag ==other.tag == "Coin"String comparison. Allocates temporary memory on every call and fails silently on typos.
  1. Why does the Unity documentation strongly recommend other.CompareTag("Coin") over other.tag == "Coin"?
  2. If you misspell a tag as "coin" (lowercase) with CompareTag, Unity throws an error alerting you that the tag does not exist. Why is an explicit error message much better for debugging than silent failure?
Analyze the Architecture ~15 min

Examine how an arcade score-tracking system separates its persistent manager from an item collector. Notice two key software patterns: the Singleton Pattern (global access + persistence) and the Trigger Callback: 

using UnityEngine;

// Persistent singleton manager tracking score across scenes
public class GameScoreKeeper : MonoBehaviour
{
    // Static reference reachable from any script without GetComponent
    public static GameScoreKeeper instance;

    [SerializeField] private int crystalScore = 0;

    private void Awake()
    {
        // Enforce singleton rule: exactly one instance exists
        if (instance == null)
        {
            instance = this;
            DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject); // Survives scene changes
        }
        else
        {
            Destroy(gameObject); // Prevent duplicate managers
        }
    }

    public void AddCrystals(int qty)
    {
        crystalScore += qty;
        Debug.Log("Crystals collected! Current tally: " + crystalScore);
    }
}

And here is how a collector script responds to an overlap event:

using UnityEngine;

// Collector component checking trigger overlaps
public class CrystalCollector : MonoBehaviour
{
    private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D hitCollider)
    {
        // 1. Identify what entered our trigger zone
        if (hitCollider.CompareTag("EnergyCrystal"))
        {
            // 2. Notify the global manager
            if (GameScoreKeeper.instance != null)
            {
                GameScoreKeeper.instance.AddCrystals(5);
            }

            // 3. Remove the picked-up object, NOT this collector!
            Destroy(hitCollider.gameObject);
        }
    }
}

Predict Before Building

  1. In CrystalCollector, what is the type of hitCollider? Why must we write hitCollider.gameObject inside Destroy() instead of passing hitCollider directly?
  2. If GameScoreKeeper.instance were a regular variable instead of static, why would CrystalCollector be unable to write GameScoreKeeper.instance directly?
Build Lab: Your Turn ~25 min

Step 1 — Set up the Coin Prefab in the Inspector. Select Assets/Prefabs/Coin:

  1. Verify it has a 2D collider (e.g. CircleCollider2D).
  2. Check the box for Is Trigger. (A pickup must be an overlap zone, not a solid wall!).
  3. At the very top of the Inspector, verify its Tag is set to Coin. (If "Coin" is not listed, click Add Tag... and create it).
Architectural Specification for StatManager.cs:
  1. File & Class Name: In Assets/Scripts/, create a new script named StatManager.cs.
  2. Global Singleton Pointer: Declare a public static StatManager manager; field.
  3. State Variable: Declare a [SerializeField] private int coins = 0; field.
  4. Awake Lifecycle: In Awake(), check if manager == null. If so, assign manager = this; and call DontDestroyOnLoad(gameObject);. If manager already exists, call Destroy(gameObject);.
  5. Public Mutation Method: Write a public void ChangeCoins(int amount) method. Inside, add amount to coins and log the new total using Debug.Log.
  6. Hierarchy Setup: In the Overworld scene, create an empty GameObject named StatManager and attach your new StatManager component to it.
Architectural Specification for PlayerController.cs:
  1. Trigger Callback: Below Update(), declare private void OnTriggerEnter2D(Collider2D other).
  2. Tag Verification: Check if other.CompareTag("Coin") is true.
  3. State Update: If it matches, check that StatManager.manager != null and call StatManager.manager.ChangeCoins(1);.
  4. Object Cleanup: Call Destroy(other.gameObject); so the collected coin vanishes from the scene.

Save both files and press Play in Unity. Walk your character into a coin! The coin should vanish upon contact, and the Unity Console will print the new coin total!

Bug Hunt: Tracing Pickup Bugs

  1. What happens if you uncheck Is Trigger on the Coin prefab? When the player walks into the coin, does OnTriggerEnter2D run?
  2. What happens if you accidentally write Destroy(gameObject) instead of Destroy(other.gameObject)? Which object vanishes from the game?
  3. What happens if you comment out Destroy(other.gameObject)? Why is a coin that gives money continuously every time you touch it a bug?
Tinker ~10 min

Tinker: Destroy vs. SetActive

  1. In Unity documentation, look up other.gameObject.SetActive(false). In PlayerController.cs, replace Destroy(other.gameObject) with other.gameObject.SetActive(false). What happens when you collect a coin?
  2. In large professional games with thousands of coins or bullets, why is disabling objects (object pooling) often preferred over destroying and creating them repeatedly?

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain the difference between a solid collider and a trigger collider
  • Explain what OnTriggerEnter2D does and identify what the other parameter refers to
  • Explain why other.CompareTag("Coin") is preferred over other.tag == "Coin"
  • Create a new C# script (StatManager.cs) and attach it to a scene GameObject
  • Commit your working coin pickup system to GitHub
